findings.title: Options-object default enables rejectOnClear even though the contract says false
findings.cause: The options destructuring defaults rejectOnClear to true when concurrency is passed as an object.
findings.impact: Calling pLimit({concurrency: 1}) changes clearQueue() semantics: pending promises are rejected with AbortError instead of being silently discarded. This is a backwards-incompatible runtime change for documented default options.
evidence: readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 document rejectOnClear as boolean with Default: false.
Focused probe output: rejected:AbortError for pLimit({concurrency: 1}) followed by clearQueue().
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const running = limit(() => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 25))); const pending = limit(() => 'pending-ran'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); let outcome = 'still-pending'; await Promise.race([pending.then(value => { outcome = 'fulfilled:' + value; }, error => { outcome = 'rejected:' + error.name; }), new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))]); await running; console.log(outcome);"

findings.title: Falsey non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation only throws when rejectOnClear is truthy and not boolean, so 0, null, and empty string are accepted.
findings.impact: Invalid configuration is silently accepted despite the documented boolean-only option, masking caller bugs and making clearQueue() behavior depend on falsey non-boolean values.
evidence: readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 specify rejectOnClear as boolean.
The git baseline at HEAD:index.js:12 checked typeof rejectOnClear unconditionally.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, null, '']) { try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}); console.log(JSON.stringify(value) + ':accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(JSON.stringify(value) + ':threw:' + error.name); } }"

findings.title: limit.map drops the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper forwards the index only when Array.isArray(iterable) is true, passing undefined for Set instances and iterator objects.
findings.impact: The documented map contract is broken for general iterables. Code using Set, Map keys, generators, or array iterators and relying on the mapper index receives undefined instead of 0, 1, 2, ...
evidence: index.js:106-113 computes iterableIsArray and passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`.
readme.md:78-84 and index.d.ts:29-43 state that mapperFunction receives the item value and its index for an iterable.
Focused probe output for Set and array iterator serialized as [["a",null],["b",null],["c",null]] and [["x",null],["y",null]], where null is JSON.stringify(undefined).
Existing tests at test.js:239-254 cover Set and array iterators but only multiply values, so they miss the missing index.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(2); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']), (value, index) => [value, index]))); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(['x', 'y'].values(), (value, index) => [value, index])));"

findings.title: limitFunction no longer forwards call-time arguments
findings.cause: The returned wrapper ignores its own arguments and always calls the wrapped function with no arguments.
findings.impact: Any consumer wrapping a parameterized function gets undefined arguments at runtime, contradicting the exported TypeScript signature and recipes that call the limited function with values.
evidence: recipes.md:161-163 calls a limited function as `limitedFetchUrl(url)`.
Focused probe output: [null,null], where JSON.stringify turned the two undefined arguments into null.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async (a, b) => [a, b], {concurrency: 1}); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limited('left', 'right')));"

findings.title: Infinity concurrency is rejected despite existing implementation support
findings.cause: validateConcurrency now requires Number.isInteger(concurrency), removing the previous Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY allowance.
findings.impact: Callers using pLimit(Infinity) as an explicit unlimited limiter now get a TypeError instead of a valid limiter. This is a behavioral regression against the existing implementation surface.
evidence: index.js:127-130 accepts only integer values greater than zero.
git baseline HEAD:index.js:123-126 accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`.
Focused probe output: threw:TypeError:Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { const limit = pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY); console.log('created', limit.concurrency); } catch (error) { console.log('threw:' + error.name + ':' + error.message); }"
